title: The Social Contract
objective: After this level you can explain the ideas of Hobbes, Locke and Rousseau.
summary: A social contract sets out the rights and duties of rulers and ruled. Hobbes traded freedom for protection, Locke grounded government in consent, and Rousseau in the general will.

cards.headline: You never signed a contract with your government. Some say you're in one anyway.
cards.body: A social contract is an agreement, real or imagined, between the people, or between the people and their rulers, setting out the rights and duties of each. Three thinkers used the idea to tackle one question: why obey a government at all? Each gave a different answer.

cards.headline: Hobbes: anything beats chaos
cards.body: Thomas Hobbes published Leviathan in 1651, after England's civil war. Picture life with no government, he said: a war of all against all, where life is "solitary, poor, nasty, brutish and short." To escape it, people hand most of their freedom to an all-powerful sovereign in exchange for peace and protection. His bargain: safety is worth a lot of freedom.

cards.headline: Locke: government works for you
cards.body: John Locke saw it differently. Even without government, he argued, people have natural rights to life, liberty and property. Government gets its legitimacy from the consent of the governed, and if rulers violate those rights, people may resist them. Remember Level 3's authority, power people accept? Locke made that acceptance the whole foundation.

cards.headline: Rousseau: rules we make together
cards.body: Jean-Jacques Rousseau, born in Geneva, opened The Social Contract (1762) with a famous line: "Man was born free, and he is everywhere in chains." His answer was the general will. People agree together to live by laws aimed at the common good, laws they make for themselves. Obeying those, he argued, is a kind of freedom.

cards.headline: Social contract: signed
learned: A social contract sets out rulers' and people's rights and duties
Hobbes: give up freedom to a sovereign for peace
Locke: natural rights, consent and a right to resist
Rousseau: laws made together by the general will

questions.prompt: According to Hobbes, what would life be like without any government?

options.label: Governed by the general will
options.rationale: The general will is Rousseau's idea.

options.label: Solitary, poor, nasty, brutish and short

questions.explanation: Hobbes pictured a war of all against all, with life "solitary, poor, nasty, brutish and short".

questions.prompt: In Locke's view, what may people do if their rulers violate their natural rights?

options.label: Nothing: the sovereign's power is absolute
options.rationale: Absolute power is Hobbes's sovereign, not Locke's.

options.label: Hand over even more freedom
options.rationale: Locke's answer runs the other way.

options.label: Leave the country forever
options.rationale: Locke's answer is a right to resist, not exile.

questions.explanation: For Locke, government rests on consent, so people may resist rulers who violate their rights to life, liberty and property.

questions.prompt: In this social contract level, which thinker is correctly paired with an idea?

options.label: Hobbes: a right to resist rulers
options.rationale: The right to resist is Locke's.

questions.explanation: Hobbes: a sovereign for protection. Locke: consent, natural rights and resistance. Rousseau: the general will.
